summary: Describes how an NFS version 4.0 client can use the fs_locations attribute, normally used for migration and replication, to discover a server's trunking capabilities. It updates RFC 7530 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A file server may have several doors. This tells a computer how to find all of them so it can use them together.

subtitle: How an NFSv4.0 client uses fs_locations to find every network path to the same file server.

tldr.problem: An NFS version 4.0 client may be able to reach one server through several network addresses, but it had no defined way to discover them or to tell them apart from copies of the data on other servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the use of the fs_locations attribute so it can list server-trunkable addresses, and tells clients to combine it with trunking detection from RFC 7931 to confirm which addresses reach the same server.
tldr.outcome: Clients can use several paths at once for higher performance and handle address changes without mistaking them for migration. It updates RFC 7530 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8587 is a Proposed Standard from May 2019 that updates RFC 7530, and the metadata lists no document obsoleting or updating it. The RFC says NFSv4.0 is specified by RFC 7530, RFC 7931 and this document read together until a consolidated replacement exists.

sections.title: Why NFSv4.0 Needs Trunking Discovery
sections.content:
NFS version 4.0 (RFC 7530) lets a file system move from one server to another, which is called migration. After a move, a client must work out whether the old and new addresses are the same server instance, whether it already holds a lease there, and whether the new server has lock state for the file system.

RFC 7931 added trunking and a way to detect it to NFSv4.0. This document adds the missing half: a way to discover candidate addresses, and rules for how clients treat the fs_locations attribute when it changes.

NFSv4.1 already had trunking detection built in (RFC 5661). The idea of server-trunkable addresses is the same in both versions.
sections.eli5: If a school has three doors, you need to know they all lead to the same school. Otherwise you might think you are visiting three different schools and get confused.

sections.title: Trunking Terminology
sections.content:
Trunking means several network addresses are connected to the same NFS server. Addresses that reach the same server instance are server-trunkable. Trunking detection confirms that two addresses reach the same server. Trunking discovery is how a client starting from one address finds other candidates.

A server endpoint is a network address combined with a connection type (RPC over a stream transport, or RPC-over-RDMA). A network address plus a root-relative pathname gives a file system network access path.

The RFC also redefines replica. Earlier documents gave each replica one access path. Here, a set of server-trunkable access paths with the same pathname counts as one replica with several paths. NFSv4.0 recognises only one kind of trunking relationship.
sections.eli5: A trunk is several roads to the same town. Discovery is finding the roads. Detection is checking they really end up in the same town.

sections.title: Location Attributes and Entries
sections.content:
The fs_locations attribute lists places where a file system can be reached. Each location entry gives a server target, either a DNS hostname or a literal network address, plus the path of the file system on that server. Entries can express trunkable addresses, replicas on other servers, migration targets or pure referrals.

A hostname in an entry is resolved by the client, and each resulting address becomes one location element made of an address and an fs_name. If the server has no pseudo-fs and exports a single file system at the root filehandle, the fs_name may be empty.

The client uses the trunking detection of RFC 7931 to confirm that the addresses really are one server. It may ignore unconfirmed relationships and treat those addresses as different servers.
sections.eli5: The list is like a signpost showing every place your files can be found. Some signs point to the same place by a different road, and some point to other places that hold a copy.

sections.title: Discovery, Detection and Connection Types
sections.content:
A client can discover trunkable addresses in two ways: a DNS query on a server hostname may return more than one address, and location entries in fs_locations may name addresses. Both are only candidates until detection confirms them.

Trunking detection requires the client to use the uniform client ID string approach from RFC 7931. A client that supports migration or trunking detection must present a uniform client ID string to all NFSv4.0 servers, or it cannot perform detection.

The attribute says nothing about which connection type to use, so clients that support several must try them. They can try serially in order of preference, which may mean long waits during a network partition, or try several at once and discard the less-preferred connections once one works.

On first access to a file system, the client should read fs_locations, then use discovery and detection to separate trunkable addresses from true replicas. Trunkable addresses can be used simultaneously for higher performance.
sections.eli5: You can find extra doors by asking the phone book or by reading the signpost. Then you check each one, and you try the different kinds of doors until one opens.

sections.title: Trunking, Migration and Replication Together
sections.content:
When the server's set of addresses changes, the outcome depends on how. If the new list is a superset, no adjustment is needed, and the client may use the extra address or keep it like a replica. If it is a subset, nothing is needed for an address the client is not using, but the client should avoid it in future. A client may keep using a removed address that is one of several paths until it gets NFS4ERR_MOVED; that is not a migration unless the last path to the server is gone.

NFS4ERR_MOVED can mean only that one address should no longer be used. Clients should not conclude migration has happened until all known addresses for that server are unusable. If a client wrongly assumes migration, it looks like a successful transparent state migration, but a lock revoked meanwhile will seem lost, and the destination server must handle its recovery with an fs-specific grace period.

To keep scanning short, servers that provide trunking information are REQUIRED to list entries usable with the current server or a migration target before those for replicas. A client can stop scanning once it sees an element with a different fs_name or an address not trunkable with the one in use.

Section 5.3 adds that when server-trunkable addresses exist, a client may assume matching file systems exist at each of them, even if they are not listed.
sections.eli5: If one door closes, you check the other doors before deciding the shop has moved. And the signpost lists the nearby doors first so you do not have to read all of it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Location information could be tampered with, sending a client to a rogue address. Without DNSSEC (RFC 4033), hostname resolution cannot be trusted, though mutual authentication through RPCSEC_GSS (RFC 7861) can reveal invalid server addresses, and TLS (RFC 8446) can also authenticate servers.

Fetching location information SHOULD use RPCSEC_GSS with integrity protection. A server SHOULD present entries for file systems on other servers using only hostnames, so the client can then query the destination with RPCSEC_GSS and integrity.

When that is not possible, for example with AUTH_SYS, the client can filter addresses to a trusted range. If neither protection nor filtering is possible, the client is best off ignoring trunking and replica information. The privacy points on uniform client strings from RFC 7931 also apply.
sections.eli5: A fake signpost could send you to a trick door. So you should check that the sign is genuine, or only trust signs from your own street.
